solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Defeat is bad in the highest degree (5)

blocks.note: read as a verb: to get the better of someone
the superlative of bad

annotation.surface: Someone declares that losing is the very worst thing that can happen.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'defeat' as a noun, but it is the verb: to worst an opponent is to get the better of them.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: the old verb means to beat someone, and the adjective is the superlative of bad.

entries.clue: Gate that may fall on cricket pitch (6)

annotation.definition2: that may fall on cricket pitch

blocks.note: a small gate, often set into a larger gate or door

blocks.clueFragment: that may fall on cricket pitch
blocks.note: in cricket, each time a batter is out this is said to fall

annotation.surface: A gate collapses onto a cricket pitch during a match.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket, a wicket is the set of stumps a batter defends; when a batter is out, commentators say a wicket has fallen.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a wicket gate is a small side gate, and in cricket wickets fall as batters are dismissed.

entries.clue: Sightseer’s drunk beer with Bruckner (12)

indicatorNotes.drunk: drunk letters stagger out of their order, as a drinker staggers

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters; 'with' just joins the two words
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A tourist has got drunk on beer while listening to the composer Bruckner.
annotation.walkthrough: Bruckner is the Austrian composer; here he only supplies letters. The ’s is short for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: a rubbernecker cranes their neck to gawp, the slang picture of a staring sightseer.

entries.clue: Video ref overturned in bad-tempered farce (8)

indicatorNotes.overturned: in a down clue, overturning something puts its letters bottom to top
indicatorNotes.in: the reversed piece is placed in the next word, which wraps round it

blocks.note: VAR = video assistant referee, used in football
testy = irritable

annotation.surface: A football pundit complains that the video referee's decision was overturned in an ill-tempered shambles.
annotation.walkthrough: Football fans know VAR decisions get overturned, which is why the word feels like part of the story rather than an instruction to the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a travesty is an absurd, grotesque mockery of what something should be.

entries.clue: Trouble had upset delicate flower (6)

indicatorNotes.upset: in a down clue, to upset something is to tip it over, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: to ail = to trouble
taken as it is

annotation.surface: Someone who had a problem has been upset by a fragile bloom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' usually signals an anagram, but here the two words simply flip end to end.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the dahlia is a garden flower whose tubers are frost-tender, hence delicate.

entries.clue: Flimsy object’s no good (4)

indicatorNotes.no: the object has no G, so the G is removed from it

blocks.note: a thing is an object; the ’s stands for 'has'
G = good, which is removed

annotation.surface: Someone dismisses a flimsy item as useless.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s means 'has': the object has no G.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in a thin excuse, one too flimsy to hold up.

entries.clue: Extremely bare area of ship to decorate (6)

indicatorNotes.Extremely: take only the extremes of the word, its first and last letters

blocks.note: the ends of BARE
a deck is a floor area on a ship

annotation.surface: A sailor is told to adorn a completely bare stretch of the ship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'bare', but it asks for that word's outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: bedeck carries the sense of adorning generously, as with flags or flowers.

entries.clue: Contact island to the west within range (9)

indicatorNotes.to the west: in an across clue, west is leftward, so the word is read right to left

blocks.note: to reach someone is to contact them
Elba, Napoleon's island of exile

annotation.surface: An instruction to get in touch with an island lying westward and close enough to reach.
annotation.walkthrough: Elba is the stock crossword island; the surface makes 'to the west' sound like a map direction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a place you are able to get to lies within your range.

entries.clue: There’s no water higher than this (7,5)

annotation.definition: There’s no water higher than this

blocks.clueFragment: There’s no water higher than this
blocks.note: the surface reading: a spring or summit that sits above every other source, as though 'higher' meant altitude
the meant reading: hotter; at normal pressure liquid water tops out at 100°C and turns to steam

annotation.surface: It sounds like a mountain spring above every other water source.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Higher' suggests height; it means temperature. Past its boiling point water is no longer water but steam.
annotation.definitionFit: Water at normal pressure cannot be heated above its boiling point and stay liquid.

entries.clue: Firm supporter in emergency committee (5)

blocks.note: Co. = company
the standard crossword 'supporter'

annotation.surface: A steadfast backer sits on a crisis committee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like an adjective describing the supporter; it is a company.
annotation.definitionFit: A proper-name definition: COBRA (Cabinet Office Briefing Room A) is the UK government's crisis committee, convened in national emergencies.

entries.clue: Anonymous card somewhat ambivalent in expression (9)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: 'somewhat' means to some extent, so only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: hidden in ambiVALENT IN Expression

annotation.surface: An unsigned card whose wording is noncommittal.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a critique of a vague message, which keeps the eye off the letters running across three words.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: valentine cards, sent on 14 February, are traditionally left unsigned.

entries.clue: Sticky stuff in mountain lake with no name (3)

indicatorNotes.with no: a lake 'with no name' has had its N (name) taken out, so that letter goes

blocks.note: a small lake in a mountain hollow, a word common in the English Lake District
N = name, which is removed

annotation.surface: Something gooey is found in a nameless lake up in the hills.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sticky stuff in mountain lake' reads as a pollution story, which hides that 'in' is only a link.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: tar is a thick, sticky black substance distilled from coal or wood.

entries.clue: Friends recalled criticism for comedy (9)

indicatorNotes.recalled: 'recalled' read as called back, so the word comes back the way it went, letters reversed

blocks.note: pals = friends
to take stick is to be criticised, British informal

annotation.surface: Friends remembered being attacked for their comic act.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' reads as remembered; it means called back.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by genre: slapstick is knockabout physical comedy, named after a clown's paddle that made a loud slap.

entries.clue: Type of key item one would prefer not to have in cupboard? (8)

annotation.definition2: item one would prefer not to have in cupboard?

blocks.note: a key filed down to open many different locks

blocks.clueFragment: item one would prefer not to have in cupboard?
blocks.note: from the idiom for a shameful secret kept hidden at home

annotation.surface: A household puzzle about keys and unwanted things lurking in cupboards.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half plays on the idiom 'a skeleton in the cupboard' (in the US, 'in the closet'), a secret you would rather not have.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a skeleton key fits many locks, and a skeleton in the cupboard is an embarrassing secret.

entries.clue: Be confused with Tuesday the last chance to eat (3-2,4)

indicatorNotes.confused: confused letters are muddled into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone mixes up their days and thinks Tuesday is their final chance for a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: A use-by date is the date printed on food packaging after which it should not be eaten; 'Tuesday' makes it look like a diary clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the date stamped on food marks the last day it is safe to eat.

entries.clue: Take apart or reverse one’s choice? (6)

blocks.note: as you would a seam, stitch by stitch
whimsically, the prefix un- plus a word for choose

annotation.surface: A question about dismantling something or changing your mind.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second definition as playful: un- plus pick, an invented undoing of a choice.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: to unpick stitching is to take it apart, and whimsically to un-pick is to undo a choice.

entries.clue: Screen image of a sailor hugging Virginia (6)

indicatorNotes.hugging: to hug is to wrap your arms round, so the sailor's letters go round Virginia's

blocks.note: a + tar, the stock crossword sailor
VA = Virginia, US state abbreviation

annotation.surface: A film still shows a sailor embracing a woman called Virginia.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Virginia' reads as a woman in a sailor's arms; it is the US state, abbreviated.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: an avatar is the figure that stands for a user on a computer or game screen.

entries.clue: Drop around for fuel (3)

indicatorNotes.around: turned around, so the word faces the other way

blocks.note: to sag is to droop or drop

annotation.surface: Someone pops round to pick up some fuel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drop around' reads as a casual visit; the phrase splits into word and indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: natural gas is burned for heating and cooking, so it is one kind of fuel.

entries.clue: Second wife longing to change (6)

blocks.note: s = second
w = wife
an itch is a restless longing

annotation.surface: A man's second wife has an urge to change things.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second wife' reads as a remarriage, but the two words are separate abbreviations.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to switch sides or plans is to change them for something else.

entries.clue: One stirring has to confront blank expression (5,4)

blocks.note: a poker stirs the fire
to face = to confront

annotation.surface: A troublemaker must meet an expressionless stare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One stirring' suggests a troublemaker; it is the fireside iron.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from cards: players keep an unreadable, blank expression so as not to give away their hand.

entries.clue: With this, king moves to castle (4)

annotation.definition: With this, king moves to castle

blocks.note: the surface reading: a monarch relocating to his fortress
the meant reading: the chess move in which the king and a corner piece swap sides; that piece is itself nicknamed the castle

annotation.surface: A monarch relocating to his fortress.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a royal moving house; in chess, castling is the one move where the king travels together with a rook, and 'castle' is also another name for the rook.
annotation.definitionFit: Castling is the only chess move in which the king moves with another piece, the rook.

entries.clue: It isn’t commonly a contaminating influence (5)

blocks.note: a dialect contraction of 'it ain't', written with an apostrophe at the front
a trace of something that spoils or corrupts

annotation.surface: Someone denies being a bad influence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Commonly' marks non-standard speech: 'tain't is how 'it ain't' is written in dialect.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: 'tain't is colloquial for it isn't, and a taint is a trace that contaminates or corrupts.

entries.clue: Can do boar in stew? Beef, rather (9)

indicatorNotes.in stew: letters in a stew are thrown together and mixed up

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A cook offers to stew wild boar, and is told beef would be better.
annotation.walkthrough: The dish in the answer is made with beef, not boar, hence 'rather'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a carbonado is a beef dish, scored and grilled or braised like the Flemish carbonnade.

entries.clue: Nick’s not connected to church (5)

blocks.note: taken as it is
CH = church; 'connected to' joins it on

annotation.surface: Nick doesn't attend church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name; it is a small cut.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are small V-shaped cuts in an edge.
